newsitem.title: FRANCE: Anti-pollution law threatens France's love of cars.
newsitem.headline: Anti-pollution law threatens France's love of cars.

text.p: The French people's love affair with the automobile collided with health fears on Friday as Environment Minister Corinne Lepage warned of likely restrictions on driving to combat soaring air pollution levels.

"We can ask factories to reduce their emissions, but we must above all convince individuals to drive less...or adopt a system allowing people to drive only every other day," Lepage told the daily Le Parisien.

"Restrictions on traffic are mandatory when pollution levels are high," the minister had earlier told officials of France's largest cities, referring to a new anti-pollution law that took effect two weeks ago.

The first area to feel the new law's bite was Lyon, France's second-largest city, which banned heavy trucks from driving through its centre on Thursday and Friday in the first restrictions ever imposed on motor vehicle use in France due to air pollution.
The new law requires France's largest cities to install pollution surveillance networks and prepare anti-pollution plans.
In the meantime, prefects -- government representatives who operate at the departmental level -- are authorised to take steps in case of a pollution emergency.
This is what happened in Lyon, when cold weather combined with a lack of wind raised pollution to health-threatening levels for three successive days.

Paul Bernard, prefect for the Rhone department which encompasses Lyon, initially banned school sports and urged elderly people to take it easy before banning heavy trucks from the motorway crossing through the city, diverting them to a ring road. It also recommended that cars skirt the city.
Pollution reached alert levels in Paris, Le Havre and Marseille this week, driven by heavy demand for electricity, increased use of fireplaces, auto exhausts and a lack of wind.
In addition to the restrictions on trucks in Lyon, some factories in the Marseille region have had to cut back on emissions of sulphur oxides.
The new anti-pollution law, which took effect on January 2, was derided by environmentalists at the time of its passage as lacking teeth since it imposed no mandatory limits on private cars.
Environmentalists had also unsuccessfully lobbied for free rides on public transit during pollution alerts.
Restrictions on private cars have long been a reality in other European states including Italy and Greece.
Passengers travelled free on buses in Florence for the first time this week as the city, one of Italy's most popular tourist attractions, battled high pollution levels by cutting car traffic.
The city council said that only cars built after 1991 with catalytic converters could travel in the city centre.
Rome's council also announced a partial block on traffic for Friday in the face of high carbon monoxide levels in the Italian capital.
